claims.claim: CRS statement of the lawmaking / internal-affairs division
claims.sourceSpan: When Congress seeks to pass a law, it uses a bill or joint resolution, which must be passed by both houses in identical form and then presented to the President for the executive's approval or disapproval. To regulate its own internal affairs, or for other purposes where authority of law is not necessary, Congress uses a concurrent resolution (requiring adoption by both houses) or a simple resolution (requiring action only in the house of origin).

claims.claim: Concurrent resolutions are not lawmaking vehicles and are not submitted to the President
claims.sourceSpan: They are not lawmaking vehicles and are not submitted to the President for approval.

claims.claim: Simple resolutions are considered only in the originating chamber and never presented elsewhere
claims.sourceSpan: Simple resolutions can only be considered in the chamber in which they originated, and they are never presented to the other chamber (or to the President).

claims.claim: REMOVED, the sweep F-FAIL (flagged low-confidence by the sweep agent, adjudicated here): "The Public Law number is assigned in order of enactment across both chambers." No stored source states this rule - 1 U.S.C. 106a covers only the Archivist receiving and preserving originals, and 1 U.S.C. 112 covers the Statutes at Large - and the stored Congress.gov law list contains a counter-example: Public Law 119-68 (H.R. 1043) is dated 2026-02-11 while Public Law 119-69 (S 222) is dated 2026-01-14. Whether that is a real ordering or a record artefact cannot be settled from anything stored, so the claim is REMOVED rather than softened. What replaces it is receipted: the Congress-plus-sequence form of the citation (from the enrolled text of P.L. 119-85), the single shared series across both chambers (derivable from the stored list), and the 1 U.S.C. 112 / 106a duties that make the public law the durable citation.

FIXED, the sweep U-FLAG and worst finding: H.Con.Res. 40 was used as the worked example of what a concurrent resolution "requires" and "could do" without disclosing that it never took effect. The corpus record shows the House vote on agreeing to the resolution FAILED 213-214 on 2026-04-16 (Roll 114) and the measure is at stage "dead". Both are now on the page.

CORRECTED: "H.J.Res. 140 ... cancelled a Bureau of Land Management mining withdrawal" - the pre-refresh page called it a mining ban. The enrolled title is quoted instead ("the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Public Land Order No. 7917 for Withdrawal of Federal Lands; Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, MN"), with the recorded signing date and public law number. The sibling blm-land-withdrawal audit established the underlying action was a LEASING withdrawal, not a mining ban; the characterisation is gone rather than restated.

SOURCED and UPGRADED, was U-FLAG: "A very low number usually signals a leadership priority" rested on nothing. The rule itself is now quoted from the primary source - House Rule XII clause 7(d) (Sec. 826b) reserves H.R. 1-10 for the Speaker and H.R. 11-20 for the Minority Leader - together with the Manual annotation that the paragraph "was added in the 119th Congress, after existing as a separate order for several Congresses." The "usually signals" framing is gone.

SOURCING NOTE, stale-secondary trap avoided: CRS R44001 (last updated January 31, 2019) says the reserved numbers go to the MAJORITY LEADER and minority leader. The 119th Congress House Manual says the Speaker and the Minority Leader. The Manual is current and primary, so the page uses the Manual for the reservation and R44001 only for the sequential-numbering mechanic, the reservation practice, and the H.R. 1040 example - each attributed to CRS with the report date in the Key Sources box.

REMOVED, unsourced: "the count restarts at the beginning of every Congress - the two-year period that begins in January of each odd-numbered year" and "Companion bills - identical text introduced in both chambers at once - receive different numbers because each chamber numbers on its own schedule." Neither the reset nor the companion-bill mechanic appears in any stored source, and the causal clause was pure inference. What survives is receipted: each form and chamber has its own designation series (R46603), so the same number in two series is two unrelated measures.

CORRECTED, shared defect with joint-resolution.html: "joint resolutions are typically used for continuing appropriations" presented as current practice. R46603 does list continuing resolutions among the uses; CRS R47106 footnote 24 supplies the currency note that in recent practice continuing appropriations are more often folded into measures carrying other legislative provisions. Both are on the page and labelled.

REWORDED, unsourced gloss: "H.R. stands for House of Representatives, not House resolution." No stored source states what the abbreviation expands to. The structural point that actually matters is receipted instead: H.R. is the House BILL series and H.Res. is a separate series that is not a lawmaking vehicle.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 1, BLOCKING, adjudicated against hman-119-rule-xii.txt and CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY): the bill-number reservation was cited as "clause 5(d)" of Rule XII in the prose, the Key Sources box, the JSON-LD citation node AND this ledger's section labels. Clause 5 is Sec. 823, "Commemoratives prohibited" - it has only paragraphs (a) and (b) and says nothing about numbers. The reservation is Sec. 826b, whose "(d)" continues the lettered run that begins at Sec. 825 ("Introduction, reference, and change of reference of public bills... 7.") and passes through Sec. 826a's "(c)". It is clause 7(d). Corrected in all four places. Two independent cross-checks agree: CRS R46603 twice cites "House Rule XII, clause 5" for the commemorative prohibition, and CRS R44001 cites "Clause 7(c) of Rule XII" for the constitutional-authority statement that immediately precedes this paragraph.

BATCH-WIDE SWEEP (2026-09-02), the systemic defect of this batch: 104 instances across all seven articles where a comma, period, semicolon or colon sat INSIDE a closing quotation mark although the source has no such character at that point. American typographic convention puts them there; this site rule does not allow it, because a span in quotation marks is a promise of verbatimness and invented punctuation inside the marks breaks that promise for a reader checking the source. Two hostile passes had each flagged one or two instances individually, which produced iterative one-at-a-time fixes and, on one span, three successive wrong repairs. The class was instead resolved MECHANICALLY: a scanner extracted every quoted span on every page, tested it against the concatenated registered sources for that article, and where the span matched only after stripping one trailing punctuation character, moved that character outside the closing quote. Per-article counts: what-is-a-committee 32, discharge-petition 22, house-rules-committee 19, bill-numbering 12, congressional-oversight 8, how-to-read-a-bill 7, joint-resolution 4. A re-scan after the sweep returns zero. No word in any quotation changed; only the position of punctuation relative to the closing mark.

SWEEP FOLLOW-UP, adjudicated not fixed: after the punctuation sweep the scanner still flags a handful of spans per page. Every one was inspected. They fall into three groups, none a defect. (1) Nested-quote renderings, where the source own internal quotation marks arrive as HTML entities or as double-backtick/double-apostrophe pairs and the page renders them as single quotes so they can sit inside a double-quoted span - already adjudicated per-article in earlier rounds. (2) Scanner pairing artefacts, where an odd number of quote characters in a paragraph makes the scanner slice across a boundary and produce a span that was never on the page. (3) The literal string article-body, which is the class attribute the scanner picks up when it strips tags. Recorded so a future audit running the same scanner does not re-open them.
